verdict: Avoid new custom-milling exposure in Raipur; lend only to clean, non-PDS millers with verified stock and no NAN arrears, and only against stock plus receivables, not against paddy procurement.
title: Raipur Rice Milling & Export: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A Raipur rice mill buys paddy, dries and de-husks it, and sells rice, bran and husk. **Cash comes from two very different pipes: government custom milling (paddy taken from NAN/FCI, rice returned against bank guarantee) and own-account trade or export.** In custom milling the miller never owns the paddy; he earns a conversion margin and his real risk is the bank guarantee and the stock he holds. In own-account milling he owns price risk on paddy and rice, and that is where working capital sits. **So when a proposal lands, first ask which pipe the cash flow comes from; if it is custom milling, the loan is effectively against a guarantee, not a trading book.**

## Where value and cash sit
Milling is a low-margin, high-turnover business: the miller's margin is thin per quintal, so profit is made on volume and on by-product recovery (bran, husk). Capex is plant and machinery plus storage, and it is lumpy. **The working-capital cycle is the whole credit story: paddy is bought in a short harvest window and rice is sold over months, so stock and receivables balloon before cash returns.** Collect from customer the actual conversion charge per quintal, the bran and husk realisation, and the stock-holding days; without these the margin cannot be judged.

## What has broken now
Local reporting is the warning. In Raipur custom milling, of 183 mills only about half a dozen returned 100% rice to NAN; 177 mills still hold 1,16,562 tonnes worth over Rs 4.66 billion, and 11 mills have deposited not a single grain [1]. The administration has issued three-day notices and threatened bank-guarantee forfeiture and sealing [1]. Earlier, 74 mills were warned with blacklisting and cause-notice [3]. Separately, an FIR was filed over Rs 5 million of rice where online records showed 1,012 quintals but only 35 quintals were found on site [2]. **This is diversion and stock-mismatch risk, not demand risk; a miller's book can look fine while the godown is empty.** The data pack flags Chhattisgarh GST growth at +2.4% versus India +6.1% and electricity demand +6.7% versus +9.5%, both local stress signals [D]. Nationally, bank credit is +26.3% YoY against output +5.1% [D], so credit is running far ahead of real activity.

## Where the growth is
Peer results show the export and branded side is where money is being made: KRBL reported its strongest-ever quarterly profitability with PAT of Rs 261 crore and EBITDA margin of 23.8% [7], and record Indian rice exports with basmati exports up about 8% to 6.5 million metric tons [4]. Amir Chand Jagdish Kumar reported net profit up 94% to Rs 366.27 million on revenue up 55% to Rs 6,646.74 million [6]. **Pursue Raipur millers with a genuine export or branded-domestic book, own paddy sourcing, and no NAN arrears; avoid pure custom-milling units and any miller on the defaulter list [1][3].**

## How to grow safely
Structure against verified stock and export receivables, not against paddy procurement. Take the NAN/FCI agreement and bank-guarantee status at sanction, and check the mill's name against the defaulter list before disbursal [1][3]. **If the proposal is custom milling, ask for the NAN deposit percentage and the guarantee amount; if the mill is below full deposit, decline.** Take monthly stock statements reconciled to online records, monthly NAN deposit progress, and quarterly GST returns. Note that the peer and rating sources are basmati-led and mostly national; they say little about Raipur specifically, so lean on first principles here.
